item.title: A new 'Danube' approach to the Hormuz Strait is in order
item.description:
During the ongoing conflict between Iran and the United States, the Arab Gulf states have borne the brunt of Iranian drone and missile strikes while incurring mounting economic costs.

With limited prospects for a U.S.-Iran settlement, Gulf states, using Oman as an interlocutor, have pursued talks with Iran aimed at ending the conflict and reopening the Strait of Hormuz to commercial shipping. This reflects a significant shift in regional dynamics: Gulf states are increasingly exploring arrangements with Iran to restore navigation without direct U.S. involvement.

Even without U.S. acquiescence, securing a negotiated agreement will be difficult. Distrust between the Arab Gulf states and Iran runs deep, rooted in historic grievances and long-term contestation for hegemony in the Middle East. The ongoing conflict has intensified hostility and resentment on both sides.

But the conflict has also revealed the Gulf states’ vulnerability while underscoring the limits of the U.S. security umbrella. Recent Houthi and Iran-backed Iraqi militia attacks on Bab Al-Mandab and Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline highlight the limits of promoting alternative shipping routes and efforts by Arab Gulf states to engineer their way out of the crisis. The need for a resolution is increasingly urgent.

A return to the status quo ante, including a return to free transit under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), seems increasingly unlikely. Replacing the norms of international maritime law with a regime allowing Iran to impose tariffs, which seems to be the basis for discussions between Oman and Iran, is untenable. While transit fees might be part of the long-term resolution, Arab Gulf states will reject any arrangement that suggests Iranian sovereignty over the strait. In fact, such an approach might prolong security tensions, with the United States feeling bound to counter Iranian claims of control with strikes or at least regular freedom of navigation operations (FONOPs) through the strait.

History offers examples of alternative approaches to maintaining trade in the context of great-power competition. The most frequently cited precedent in this regard is the 1936 Montreux Convention, which continues to govern transit through Turkey’s Bosphorus and Dardanelles. The convention offers useful lessons for Hormuz, particularly in its approach to foreign naval access. But a more applicable model may come from a less obvious place: the Danube River after the Crimean War.

The 1856 Treaty of Paris established the European Commission of the Danube amid intense regional competition in Europe. Unable to secure an agreement on the use of the river, the signatories devised an approach that handed responsibility for navigability and shipping safety on the lower Danube to an independent international organization.

While the signatories maintained oversight through a board, the commission operated independently, even charging tolls and raising debt to fund trade infrastructure expansion. By delegating management of the river to an independent body, competing powers reduced potential flashpoints while allowing all of Europe to benefit from trade along the Danube, which runs from what is now southwestern Germany to the Black Sea coast between modern Romania and Ukraine. Initially seen as a temporary expedient, the commission remained in place for over 85 years.

A similar Strait of Hormuz Commission could help return stability and trade flows to the region. The institution could be overseen by a board representing the eight countries bordering the Gulf. Major trading partners in Asia and Europe, together with the United States, could participate through an advisory body, giving them influence and incentives to cooperate with the scheme without giving them a veto.

Initially, the commission would have a narrow mandate: ensuring safe commercial passage; coordinating escort, rescue, and environmental-response services; and maintaining facilities required for these functions. To reduce the risk of military miscalculation, the commission could require naval vessels to report intended transit and share that information with member states, as required under Montreux. Its costs could be covered by reasonable service charges, tolls or member financing.

The Danube approach would allow the institutional structure and responsibilities of the commission to develop incrementally. An initial agreement could establish principles and procedures for commercial transit, maritime safety and communication among the parties. More sensitive functions, from military deconfliction of the strait to support for broader regional infrastructure development, could be added as confidence in the commission develops.

The governing principle would be shared management without shared sovereignty. Neither Iran nor Oman would relinquish territorial claims, and the commission would acquire no sovereignty over the strait. Its authority would extend only to the management and security of navigation through the strait. The objective would not be to resolve the region’s rivalries, but to insulate one vital shared interest from them.

Crucially, establishing such a commission would not have to await a comprehensive settlement of the Gulf’s wider conflicts. Indeed, that would defeat much of its purpose. Concentrating on the narrower shared interest of restoring predictable commercial transit would give the countries of the region a platform for practical collaboration and building confidence. If successful, the commission would provide a foundation for constructive dialogue on more contentious issues, including Iran’s nuclear program, eliminating political interference and support for proxy groups, and resolving longstanding territorial disputes. The commission would not have a mandate to resolve these disputes, but it could help build trust and the habits of cooperation needed to address them through other diplomatic channels.

Critics will argue that negotiating such an arrangement rewards Iran for challenging international maritime law and using its geographical position to extract concessions. Others will voice concern about the precedent for strategic waterways such as the Strait of Malacca and Bab Al-Mandab.

Both concerns are legitimate. But insisting on a legal regime that can no longer reliably secure transit does not in itself reopen Hormuz. Nor would shared management of the strait require abandoning the principles of freedom of navigation. Ultimately, as the international rules-based order comes under growing pressure, upholding universal principles like freedom of navigation may require new arrangements that address local contexts and create incentives for neighboring states — including rivals — to uphold them.

For Iran and the Gulf states, the choice is ultimately pragmatic. Cooperation after years of distrust and the imposition of more recent wounds inflicted by the current conflict will be difficult. But a jointly established commission could reopen the strait for sustained trade while helping to address the parties’ core security and economic concerns.

More important, it would establish a model for the Gulf’s emerging security order: regionally-owned, internationally-supported, and built around the institutional management of shared interests rather than dependence on any single outside power.

item.title: America's Counter-Drone Authority Is Real, The Capacity Isn't Yet
item.description:
Here is a number worth sitting with: federal teams seized roughly 700 drones around World Cup venues this summer. Seven hundred — at one tournament, in one season, with the best-resourced counter-drone units in the world on the field. That figure is a success story and a warning in the same breath: the threat volume is enormous, and the federal government cannot be the only team suiting up for it.

Until this year, it legally had to be. The power to disable a hostile drone belonged to a short list of federal agencies, which left a state trooper at a stadium gate or a corrections captain watching an aircraft hover over his yard with nothing but binoculars and a report form. Congress ended that with the SAFER SKIES Act in December's defense bill, and the DHS-Justice framework implementing it has been in force since July 1: state, local, tribal, and territorial police and corrections agencies that complete federal training and certification, on approved equipment, can now track a threatening drone and — against a credible threat — take it out of the sky above major venues, critical infrastructure, and prisons.

And in the past week, Washington has shown it means to deliver. The Justice Department announced that the FBI's counter-drone training center in Huntsville will double its capacity. DHS's Science and Technology Directorate put commercial counter-drone systems through operational testing alongside state and local officers. The Pentagon selected four directed-energy systems for a homeland counter-drone pilot. This is what implementation momentum looks like, and the departments deserve real credit for it.

Now the hard truth: doubling a small number produces a small number. The Huntsville center's first class, last fall, held twelve officers, and it remains the only place in America where a state or local officer can earn the legal right to bring down a drone. More than 18,500 agencies are now eligible for these authorities. Against that denominator, even a doubled schoolhouse leaves the vast majority of American communities exactly where they were — watching — while the Super Bowl arrives in four months and the Los Angeles Olympics in under two years. Our prisons cannot wait either: drone incidents at federal correctional facilities rose twentyfold in six years, and state systems from South Carolina to Georgia are logging airborne contraband runs by the hundreds.

What turns momentum into coverage is money, sustained past the current news cycle. Congress should fund training at the scale of the authority it created: regional and satellite course delivery so a deputy in Phoenix is not waiting on a classroom seat in Alabama, instructor pipelines that multiply the schoolhouse instead of merely enlarging it, and a certification target tied to the event calendar that oversight committees actually track. Just as important, the FEMA counter-UAS grant program — $500 million across 2026 and 2027, built around the World Cup — should not sunset with the tournament that inspired it. The threat is not leaving when the fans do.

Governors have their own homework, and fewer excuses than ever: the grant rules push at least 97 percent of awarded funds down to local and tribal agencies within 45 days. The money is designed to reach the street. States should name a lead agency, compete for those dollars this cycle, and put their corrections systems and stadium districts first in line for certified teams.

Over more than twenty years in federal homeland security — the last of them leading U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement — I watched threats outrun statutes again and again. This time the statute arrived first, and this past week proved the executive branch intends to use it. The remaining question belongs to Congress and fifty governors: whether a nation that just confiscated 700 drones at a single sporting event will fund protection for everyone else. Authority without capacity is a promise. Appropriations are how promises get kept.

item.title: A gen Z protest movement could be about to oust Serbia’s strongman. Here’s why that will shake Europe | Misha Glenny
item.description:
Student activists seem set to defeat Aleksandar Vučić at the ballot box this Sunday. The EU should never have written off Serbian democracy

History may not be about to repeat itself in Serbia, but it is beginning to rhyme. Just over a quarter of a century ago, Serbian citizens turned out to vote in large numbers to inflict a historic defeat on the then strongman in Belgrade, Slobodan Milošević, who was seeking re-election as president. He lost despite his extensive control over the media, the judiciary and the security forces. When he was reluctant to leave office, Serbs poured on to the streets in their hundreds of thousands, finally forcing him to go.

On Sunday, a new generation could have the decisive voice in an equally fateful election, this time for the national parliament. Today’s strongman, Aleksandar Vučić, recently resigned as president to fight the election with the aim of swapping the locus of power from the presidency to the prime minister’s office.

Most voters in key states want to block US arms transfers to Israel
item.description:
A majority of likely voters in each of six key swing states — Georgia, Iowa, Maine, North Carolina, Ohio, and Texas — say they approve of measures to block the transfer of bombs to Israel, according to a new poll released Wednesday by the Institute for Middle East Understanding (IMEU) and conducted by the YouGov data analytics firm.

The poll also found that majorities or strong pluralities of 3,200 respondents in the six states favor “cutting $3.3 billion in taxpayer-funded weapons to Israel” and believe the war in Iran benefits Israel more than the United States.

As in other recent polls, the new survey, which was conducted from late September to mid-October, found that self-identified Democrats and Independents were significantly more likely to oppose more military transfers to Israel than self-identified Republicans in each state, although at least one-third of Republicans in all of the states except North Carolina (26%) said they supported blocking bombs to Israel.

The highest percentage of Republicans taking that position was found in Maine, where 45% said they opposed more such transfers. Incumbent Sen. Susan Collins, who is in a tight race against a Democrat who has criticized U.S. military aid and sales to Israel, voted against a resolution to ban the transfer of 1,000- and 2,000-pound bombs to Israel April 15, the last time the Senate voted on the issue. That vote marked the first time that a majority of Senate Democrats (36 of 46 members of the caucus) voted to block weapons transfers to Israel.

IMEU is a pro-Palestinian organization. YouGov, which fielded the survey, is considered a reliable pollster, and the poll’s questions were posed in neutral terms.

All six of the states polled by YouGov are considered critical to Democratic hopes of gaining control of the Senate in the November 3 midterm elections. Of the six Senate seats that are contested in them this year, only one is currently held by a Democrat, Jon Ossoff of Georgia.

The survey suggests that support for Israel and the Iran war among Republicans could prove a liability in next month’s midterm elections. As RS reported last week, some Republican Senate candidates in battleground states have tried to distance themselves from the Iran war, though few have voted in Congress to end or restrict it.

While the survey did not ask respondents how much weight they would accord U.S. military support for Israel and the war in Iran in deciding how they will vote in this year’s senatorial elections, it comes as a series of other polls have shown unprecedented popular disapproval of Israel’s conduct in its three-year-old war in Gaza and persistent strong opposition (55%) to the ongoing U.S. conflict in Iran. A pair of recent polls also indicated that voters are more concerned about the Iran war than immigration or crime, two issues that Republicans tend to dominate.

On whether they approve or disapprove of “Senate measures to block the transfer of bombs to Israel,” 65% of Maine respondents said they approved, while only 22% said they disapproved. In Georgia, the split was 55% approved, and 28% disapproved; in Iowa, the split was 56%-24%; North Carolina, 51%-30%; Ohio, 57%-31%; and Texas 54%-30%.

Asked about “cutting $3.3 billion in taxpayer-funded weapons to Israel” that the U.S. provides each year, 52% of Georgia respondents said they approved, while 34% said they disapproved. In Iowa, the split was 59%-26%; in Maine, 57%-30%; North Carolina, 48%-34%; Ohio, 54%-37%; and Texas, 52%-34%.

Asked which country the Iran war benefits the most, 50% of Georgia voters said Israel, while 28% said the U.S.; in Iowa, the split was 54% Israel, 21% the U.S.; Maine, 59%-19%; North Carolina, 52%-23%; Ohio, 49%-27%; and Texas, 51%-25%.

item.title: What's the point of a permanent US military base in Poland?
item.description:
When Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, the United States deployed almost 5,000 troops to Poland, doubling the number that had already been stationed there. The reinforcements were sent mostly to southeastern Poland, close to the border with Ukraine, and their task was to deter further Russian aggression.

Warsaw welcomed the move but uncertainty persisted: the troops were deployed on a rotational, not permanent, basis. Now Poland, which prides itself on being the staunchest U.S. ally in Europe, wants more.

For many months, the center-left government and the right-wing presidential administration have been in talks with the Trump administration to set up a permanent U.S. military base in Poland. Polish Deputy Defense Minister Cezary Tomczyk recently said the decision is “imminent” and should be made no later than December, while Elbridge Colby, the undersecretary of defense for policy, wrote that there is an “ongoing exploration of potential opportunities for permanent basing of U.S. forces in Poland.” According to Stanisław Wziątek, another Polish deputy defense minister, the prospective base could accommodate up to 5,000 additional troops.

Details of the negotiations are scarce, but expectations in Poland run high. The government sees the Trump administration’s decision as a test of whether it is willing to put additional pressure on Russia. The presidential administration wants to capitalize on President Karol Nawrocki’s good relations with President Donald Trump to secure a favor in the form of a permanent U.S. military base. Both sides would be massively disappointed should the U.S. eventually pass on the project.

There is reason to believe, however, that the long-awaited base is not as crucial to Poland’s security as officials in Warsaw like to think. The very fact that the talks between Poland and the United States have dragged on for many months suggests that there is little sense of urgency, at least in the White House, and that the threat of Russian attack on Poland is not imminent.

For Poland, this should be a clear indication that the key to its security lies neither in amassing U.S. troops on its territory, nor in currying favor with Trump – who may change his mind at any time – but rather in adopting a more independent-minded attitude, which would allow for more political flexibility and a greater focus on its own military potential.

Russian threat, American retreat


It is true that the Russian drones and fighter jets regularly fly close to the Polish border and occasionally violate Polish airspace. It is also true that Russia has carried out sabotage operations in Poland, according to Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk. But there is no serious indication that Moscow intends to, or is able to, invade Poland.

Even if Russia wanted to subjugate Poland, one should bear in mind that since 2022, hundreds of thousands of Russian troops have failed to break through the front lines in the Donbas, a region located more than 600 miles away from the Polish-Ukrainian border. It is also not difficult to figure out that invading Poland would make absolutely no sense for Russian President Vladimir Putin at a time when he is hoping to reach a deal with Trump.

The sluggish pace of U.S.-Polish negotiations stems from the Trump administration’s National Security Strategy. Since the beginning of 2025, the United States has largely focused on reducing its commitments and cutting down the U.S. military presence in Europe, not shoring it up. In December, the Pentagon is expected to conclude its review of the U.S. force posture in Europe, and the most likely result is the reduction in troop levels on the continent. It is plausible that the project of a permanent base in Poland will be scrapped too, or at least put on the shelf. After all, that would be consistent with the Pentagon’s concept of “NATO 3.0,” which aims to shift the responsibility for conventional deterrence to European allies.

There is a possibility, of course, that the White House goes forward with a permanent base in Poland. This would likely reflect a short-term victory by the hawks in the administration and Congress who want to put more pressure on Russia. Alternatively, this could be Trump's gesture toward Nawrocki, a fellow nationalist, whom he praises lavishly. Either way, Polish officials should not delude themselves into thinking that such a decision would be made out of concern for Poland’s security in particular.

Time to change gears


Given these circumstances, Polish officials should think about their country’s security in a more unorthodox and open-minded way. Poland is a dynamic, rapidly-developing economy that needs three things to prosper: physical security, political stability and a high level of investment. There is a serious risk, however, that a protracted “forever” war across the border, coupled with ever-increasing tensions between Russia and Europe, will make it much more difficult to achieve these goals.

The likelihood of such a bleak scenario is all the more probable because Poland now believes that the conflict between Russia and the West is inevitable and that the only way to ensure its own security is through military means. Warsaw heavily invests in military equipment while senior government officials declare that they want to have the largest army in Europe. Poland’s defense budget is approaching 5% of its GDP, and the slogan “if you want peace, prepare for war” can be heard almost everywhere.

But the fact that this militarization occurs in a total absence of European-led diplomatic efforts aimed at reducing tensions and ending the war in Ukraine makes Poland more, not less, vulnerable. Officials in Warsaw may not see it this way, but relations between Europe and Russia have steadily been spiraling into the so-called security dilemma, an international relations theory premised on the observation that defensive preparations by one side are almost inevitably viewed as offensive by its enemy. The crux of security dilemma is that no amount of additional equipment or troops can make either side feel safer. Once the downward spiral begins, things can very easily get out of control. And that is exactly what is happening right now.

So what might a new approach to Polish security look like?

In the foreseeable future, military partnership with the United States will remain a bedrock of Polish foreign policy, but from Warsaw’s perspective it would be a mistake to indefinitely rely on American equipment and security guarantees.

In the current geopolitical environment, Poland would be wise to speed up the development of its own military industry, especially in the field of drones, automation and AI. This could make it more resistant to a threat posed by Russia's hybrid operations or any other future threats.

But first and foremost, Poland should recognize an urgent need to invest in an active and flexible diplomacy aimed at reducing hostility and tensions with the country it fears the most.

This would be no easy task, and, most likely, it would not yield any concrete result at the beginning. But it would be a far more prudent path than desperately seeking a permanent U.S. lifeline at a time when the U.S. is pulling back from Europe.

item.title: Exclusive-Senior UAE diplomat Lana Nusseibeh enters race for UN chief
item.description:
By Maha El Dahan

DUBAI, Oct 21 (Reuters) - Senior UAE diplomat Lana Nusseibeh entered the race to become the next United Nations secretary-general on Wednesday, injecting a prominent Middle Eastern candidate into a contest that has struggled to produce a consensus choice among the Security Council’s most powerful members.

Nusseibeh, a former UAE ambassador to the UN for more than a decade, told Reuters she would seek to restore the world body’s role as a diplomatic problem-solver at a time of mounting global crises.

item.title: UAE nominates official to lead UN
item.description:
The UAE nominated Wednesday its foreign ministry official Lana Nusseibeh to run in the contest to lead the UN as none of the six existing candidates has emerged as a clear front-runner.

Lana Nusseibeh is a well-regarded minister of state at the United Arab Emirates foreign ministry, having previously represented Abu Dhabi at the UN.

item.title: US orders departure of diplomats from Saudi Arabia amid Houthi strikes
item.description:
JERUSALEM/ISTANBUL/DUBAI, Oct 21 (Reuters) - The US State Department has ordered some diplomats and family members to depart from its missions in Saudi Arabia and is planning to move out family members from a number of other US missions in the Gulf, US officials told Reuters.

State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said in a post on X that the department ordered the departure of "non-emergency US government employees and their family members in Saudi Arabia only" amid attacks by the Iran-alignedHouthis in Yemen on civilian targets in the country.

item.title: US sanctions Greece-, Panama-based law firm over aid to Iranian shipping
item.description:
WASHINGTON, Oct 21 (Reuters) - The US Treasury Department imposed sanctions on Wednesday on Karnakis & Karnakis, a law firm based in Greece and Panama, saying it had for years provided legal assistance to Iranian shipping networks.

The US Financial Crimes Enforcement Network also issued an administrative subpoena to advance an investigation into a Greek bank over potential ties to Iran, according to a Treasury statement, which did not name the bank.

item.title: After Syria war, Druze in Golan Heights warm to Israel

"It's crucial for all Israeli citizens to vote," said Damaqsi, from the Golan Heights town of Ein Qiniye. "It's a right, but it's also an honour."
